title: Jonah and the Harvest
premise: Hospice nurse Oscar Winterbourne has spent years recording the strange phenomenon she calls 'the count'—the dying ticking down numbers only they can hear, always reaching zero at the moment of death. When an excavation crew on the Winterbourne family estate unearths a door sealed from the inside, the count begins spreading to the living, and Oscar realizes her decades of documentation contain the pattern that predicts who it will take next. To save the last of the Winterbourne line—her estranged employers—she must break her vow of invisibility, expose what the family buried generations ago, and let the dead finally be counted. In the end, Oscar opens the door from the outside, offering herself as the final entry in a ledger that has been waiting for someone willing to read it aloud.
about_author: Emrys Brightwater is the pen name of a former palliative care volunteer turned novelist who writes horror rooted in the quiet terrors of institutions and inheritance. They live in a converted chapel on the coast, where they keep meticulous notebooks they claim are purely for research.

chapters.title: The Backwards Men
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At Hollowmere Hospice, Oscar records patient Edmund Vail counting down from ninety-one, documenting his terror in her ledger as he dies precisely at zero. She introduces her ritual: documentation is prayer, invisibility is safety. Emotional beat: eerie competence masking deep loneliness; the reader learns the count is real before anyone else believes it.

chapters.title: Winterbourne House
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar takes a private nursing post at decaying Winterbourne House, caring for matriarch Agnes Winterbourne, who is dying but refuses to count—or pretends not to. The house is being partially demolished for a new foundation. Emotional beat: unease beneath professional calm; Agnes flinches at every mention of the excavation.

chapters.title: What the Ground Keeps
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The crew's backhoe strikes something at dawn: a stone door, iron-banded, its hinges on the inside. The foreman finds no record of any structure there. That night, Agnes whispers a number—forty-four—and begs Oscar to write it down. Emotional beat: dread arrives quietly; the first living person begins the count.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Deaths
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with excerpts from her old ledgers. Reviewing twenty years of notes, Oscar discovers every counted death traced geographically back toward the Winterbourne estate—a radius tightening over decades. Emotional beat: horrified revelation that her careful records were evidence all along, and she was the only one collecting it.

chapters.title: The Nephew
chapters.summary: Julian Winterbourne's POV. Julian, Agnes's heir, arrives from London to oversee the demolition, pragmatic and dismissive of his aunt's ravings. He orders the door left alone until lawyers clear it. Emotional beat: cold denial; Julian sees the house as an asset, not a grave, establishing him as both obstacle and victim-to-be.

chapters.title: Forty-Three
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Agnes counts down nightly now, one number per night, lucid between counts and desperate. She tells Oscar about 'the tithe'—a family debt paid in deaths since 1847—and that the door was sealed from within by those who went down willingly. Emotional beat: confession as burden; Agnes passes the weight of knowing to Oscar.

chapters.title: Parish Records
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the village archive, Oscar finds the harvest rolls: every generation, the estate recorded a 'harvest' of names, always ending when the count reached zero. The last entry, 1919, lists seven names—the seven who sealed themselves below. Emotional beat: scholarly dread hardening into resolve; justice outside the law takes shape as Oscar decides the record must be completed, not hidden.

chapters.title: The Crew Hears It
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: foreman Danny Okafor and night watchman. Workers begin hearing faint counting under the soil; two quit. Danny, skeptical, stays for hazard pay and starts hearing his own number. Emotional beat: contagion of fear; the phenomenon escapes the family bloodline, raising stakes beyond inheritance.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Noise
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian finds his grandfather's letters describing how each heir must 'keep the count honest'—and how his father fled, breaking the chain. Julian realizes the demolition wasn't his idea; the letters suggest the house summoned him home. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into complicity; Julian understands he inherited a debt, not an estate.

chapters.title: Zero at Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A former hospice colleague calls: three of Oscar's old patients died the same night, all counting, all reaching zero together. The count has jumped the radius entirely. Oscar burns her first ledger page in panic, then retrieves it from the ash—documentation is prayer, and prayers can't be retracted. Emotional beat: crisis of faith in her own ritual.

chapters.title: Agnes's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Agnes, at thirty-eight, explains the rule she finally admits: the count pauses only while a Winterbourne lives above ground who knows the names. Knowledge is the tether. If she dies with the names unspoken, the harvest takes freely. Emotional beat: tender, terrible intimacy; nurse and patient become co-conspirators against time itself.

chapters.title: The Names Below
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Behind the wainscoting, Oscar finds the original harvest roll with the seven names of 1919—and an eighth column, blank, labeled 'the reader.' Whoever speaks the names aloud at the door becomes part of the accounting. Emotional beat: dawning sacrifice; Oscar sees the shape of the ending and doesn't look away.

chapters.title: Danny's Number
chapters.summary: Danny Okafor's POV. Danny's count reaches single digits; he barricades himself in the site office and calls Julian, begging. Julian, shaken, finally reads Oscar's ledgers overnight and finds the pattern she's mapped for twenty years. Emotional beat: skeptic converted by evidence; the alliance forms out of desperation rather than trust.

chapters.title: Terms of Settlement
chapters.summary: Oscar and Julian's alternating POV. They attempt a legal exorcism of sorts: filing the harvest roll as a public record, holding a reading on the lawn, speaking the seven names to the open air. The count stutters—then accelerates, angry. Emotional beat: hope punished; institutional justice fails because the debt was never legal, only owed.

chapters.title: Thirty-One
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Agnes reaches thirty-one and stops eating, choosing to spend her remaining nights dictating everything she knows about the seven below—who they were, why they volunteered, what they were promised. Emotional beat: elegiac; the horror humanizes into history, and memory becomes the only currency that matters.

chapters.title: What Was Promised
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, dreamlike interlude. Through Agnes's dictation and the roll's marginalia, the 1919 harvest emerges: famine wages, a landlord's arithmetic, seven workers who traded their names for their families' survival. The door was sealed from inside because they chose to stop being counted among the living. Emotional beat: righteous anger; the true monster is the inheritance system itself.

chapters.title: Julian Descends
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Refusing to let Oscar pay the eighth name, Julian goes to the door alone at night with the roll in hand, intending to read the names himself. He hears voices answering in kind—his own ancestors, keeping their side of the bargain. Emotional beat: courage as atonement; the heir finally accepts the inheritance.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar follows Julian down. Together they speak all seven names at the threshold; the door unseals with a sound like a held breath released. But the blank eighth column glows in Oscar's mind, and Agnes's distant voice, upstairs, reaches nine. Emotional beat: awe and vertigo; the climax begins as accounting, not combat.

chapters.title: Eight
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Below the door lies not a crypt but a harvest floor—names carved in rows, generations deep, the whole family's debt made visible. The count demands completion. Oscar steps forward to give her name, arguing that a witness who documented everything owes herself to the record. Emotional beat: sacrificial clarity; Oscar chooses meaning over invisibility.

chapters.title: Agnes at Zero
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. As Oscar speaks her name, Agnes dies upstairs at zero—and the count breaks, the harvest satisfied by a full accounting rather than a body. The door closes gently behind them, sealing from the outside this time. Julian carries Oscar up through collapsing earth as the house settles around them. Emotional beat: climax resolving into mercy; the ledger balances without claiming a life.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, weeks later. The estate passes to Julian, who converts Winterbourne House into a hospice and hires Oscar as its director. The harvest roll hangs framed in the lobby, eight columns complete. No one counts anymore—or if they do, they reach no number at all. Emotional beat: quiet restoration; justice achieved through memory, not law.

chapters.title: The New Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, closing chapter. On her first night at the hospice, a dying patient smiles and says, 'Someone finally read us our names.' Oscar opens a fresh notebook and writes the date—not a countdown, but a beginning. Final image: documentation as prayer answered. Emotional beat: peace earned through horror; the story ends where it began, at a bedside, but listening differently.
